label: algorithm
summary: NIST DADS defines algorithm as: A computable set of steps to achieve a desired result.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: algorithm

label: data structure
summary: NIST DADS defines data structure as: An organization of information, usually in memory, for better algorithm efficiency , such as queue , stack , linked list , heap , dictionary , and tree , or conceptual unity, such as the name and address of a person. It may include redundant information, such as length of the list or number of nodes in a subtree .

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: dataStructure

label: search
summary: NIST DADS defines search as: Look for a value or item in a data structure. There are dozens of algorithms, data structures, and approaches.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: search

label: sort
summary: NIST DADS defines sort as: Arrange items in a predetermined order. There are dozens of algorithms, the choice of which depends on factors such as the number of items relative to working memory, knowledge of the orderliness of the items or the range of the keys , the cost of comparing keys vs. the cost of moving items, etc. Most algorithms can be implemented as an in-place sort , and many can be implemented so they are stable , too. Formal Definition: The sort operation may be defined in terms of an initial array, S, of N items and a final array, S′, as follows. S′ i ≤ S′ i+1 , 0 < i < N (the items are in order) and S′ is a permutation of S.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: sort

label: binary search
summary: NIST DADS defines binary search as: Search a sorted array by repeatedly dividing the search interval in half. Begin with an interval covering the whole array. If the value of the search key is less than the item in the middle of the interval, narrow the interval to the lower half. Otherwise narrow it to the upper half. Repeatedly check until the value is found or the interval is empty.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: binarySearch

label: linear search
summary: NIST DADS defines linear search as: Search an array or list by checking items one at a time. Also known as sequential search.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: linearSearch

label: merge sort
summary: NIST DADS defines merge sort as: A sort algorithm that splits the items to be sorted into two groups, recursively sorts each group, and merges them into a final, sorted sequence. Run time is Θ (n log n).

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: mergesort

label: quicksort
summary: NIST DADS defines quicksort as: Pick an element from the array (the pivot), partition the remaining elements into those greater than and less than this pivot, and recursively sort the partitions. There are many variants of the basic scheme above: to select the pivot, to partition the array, to stop the recursion or switch to another algorithm for small partitions, etc.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: quicksort

label: heapsort
summary: NIST DADS defines heapsort as: A sort algorithm that builds a heap , then repeatedly extracts the maximum item. Run time is O(n log n) .

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: heapSort

label: insertion sort
summary: NIST DADS defines insertion sort as: Sort by repeatedly taking the next item and inserting it into the final data structure in its proper order with respect to items already inserted. Run time is O(n 2 ) because of moves. Also known as linear insertion sort.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: insertionSort

label: selection sort
summary: NIST DADS defines selection sort as: A sort algorithm that repeatedly searches remaining items to find the least one and moves it to its final location. The run time is Θ(n²) , where n is the number of elements. The number of swaps is O(n) .

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: selectionSort

label: bubble sort
summary: NIST DADS defines bubble sort as: Sort by comparing each adjacent pair of items in a list in turn, swapping the items if necessary, and repeating the pass through the list until no swaps are done. Also known as sinking sort, exchange sort.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: bubblesort

label: counting sort
summary: NIST DADS defines counting sort as: A 2-pass sort algorithm that is efficient when the number of distinct keys is small compared to the number of items. The first pass counts the occurrences of each key in an auxiliary array , and then makes a running total so each auxiliary entry is the number of preceding keys. The second pass puts each item in its final place according to the auxiliary entry for that key.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: countingsort

label: radix sort
summary: NIST DADS defines radix sort as: A multiple pass distribution sort algorithm that distributes each item to a bucket according to part of the item's key beginning with the least significant part of the key. After each pass, items are collected from the buckets, keeping the items in order, then redistributed according to the next most significant part of the key.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: radixsort

label: bucket sort
summary: NIST DADS defines bucket sort as: A distribution sort where input elements are initially distributed to several buckets based on an interpolation of the element's key . Each bucket is sorted if necessary, and the buckets' contents are concatenated. Also known as bin sort.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: bucketsort

label: bintree
summary: NIST DADS defines bintree as: A regular decomposition k-d tree for region data.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: bintree

label: binary search tree
summary: NIST DADS defines binary search tree as: A binary tree where every node's left subtree has keys less than the node's key, and every right subtree has keys greater than the node's key.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: binarySearchTree

label: AVL tree
summary: NIST DADS defines AVL tree as: A balanced binary search tree where the height of the two subtrees ( children ) of a node differs by at most one. Look-up, insertion, and deletion are O(log n) , where n is the number of nodes in the tree.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: avltree

label: red-black tree
summary: NIST DADS defines red-black tree as: A nearly-balanced tree that uses an extra bit per node to maintain balance. No leaf is more than twice as far from the root as any other. Formal Definition: A red-black tree with n internal nodes has height at most 2log 2 (n+1). Also known as symmetric binary B-tree.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: redblack

label: heap
summary: NIST DADS defines heap as: A complete tree where every node has a key more extreme (greater or less) than or equal to the key of its parent . Usually understood to be a binary heap .

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: heap

label: queue
summary: NIST DADS defines queue as: A collection of items in which only the earliest added item may be accessed. Basic operations are add (to the tail ) or enqueue and delete (from the head ) or dequeue. Delete returns the item removed. Also known as "first-in, first-out" or FIFO. Formal Definition: It is convenient to define delete or dequeue in terms of remove and a new operation, front. The operations new(), add(v, Q), front(Q), and remove(Q) may be defined with axiomatic semantics as follows. new() returns a queue front(add(v, new())) = v remove(add(v, new())) = new() front(add(v, add(w, Q))) = front(add(w, Q)) remove(add(v, add(w, Q))) = add(v, remove(add(w, Q))) where Q is a queue and v and w are values. Also known as FIFO.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: queue

label: stack
summary: NIST DADS defines stack as: A collection of items in which only the most recently added item may be removed. The latest added item is at the top. Basic operations are push and pop. Often top and isEmpty are available, too. Also known as "last-in, first-out" or LIFO. Formal Definition: The operations new(), push(v, S), top(S), and popoff(S) may be defined with axiomatic semantics as follows. new() returns a stack popoff(push(v, S)) = S top(push(v, S)) = v where S is a stack and v is a value. The pop operation is a combination of top, to return the top value, and popoff, to remove the top value. The predicate isEmpty(S) may be defined with the following additional axioms. isEmpty(new()) = true isEmpty(push(v, S)) = false Also known as LIFO.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: stack

label: linked list
summary: NIST DADS defines linked list as: A list implemented by each item having a link to the next item. Also known as singly linked list.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: linkedList

label: doubly linked list
summary: NIST DADS defines doubly linked list as: A variant of a linked list in which each item has a link to the previous item as well as the next. This allows easily accessing list items backward as well as forward and deleting any item in constant time. Also known as two-way linked list, symmetrically linked list.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: doublyLinkedList

label: graph
summary: NIST DADS defines graph as: A set of items connected by edges . Each item is called a vertex or node . Formally, a graph is a set of vertices and a binary relation between vertices, adjacency. Formal Definition: A graph G can be defined as a pair (V,E), where V is a set of vertices, and E is a set of edges between the vertices E ⊆ {(u,v) | u, v ∈ V}. If the graph is undirected, the adjacency relation defined by the edges is symmetric , or E ⊆ {{u,v} | u, v ∈ V} (sets of vertices rather than ordered pairs). If the graph does not allow self-loops , adjacency is irreflexive .

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: graph

label: Dijkstra's algorithm
summary: NIST DADS defines Dijkstra's algorithm as: An algorithm to find the shortest paths from a single source vertex to all other vertices in a weighted, directed graph . All weights must be nonnegative.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: dijkstraalgo

label: Bellman-Ford algorithm
summary: NIST DADS defines Bellman-Ford algorithm as: An efficient algorithm to solve the single-source shortest-path problem . Weights may be negative. The algorithm initializes the distance to the source vertex to 0 and all other vertices to ∞. It then does V-1 passes (V is the number of vertices) over all edges relaxing, or updating, the distance to the destination of each edge. Finally it checks each edge again to detect negative weight cycles , in which case it returns false. The time complexity is O(VE) , where E is the number of edges. Also known as Ford-Bellman.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: bellmanford

label: topological sort
summary: NIST DADS defines topological sort as: To arrange items when some pairs of items have no comparison, that is, according to a partial order .

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: topologicalSort

label: minimum spanning tree
summary: NIST DADS defines minimum spanning tree as: A minimum-weight tree in a weighted graph which contains all of the graph's vertices . Also known as MST, shortest spanning tree, SST.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: minimumSpanningTree

label: Prim-Jarnik algorithm
summary: NIST DADS defines Prim-Jarnik algorithm as: Compute a minimum spanning tree by beginning with any vertex as the current tree . At each step add a least edge between any vertex not in the tree and any vertex in the tree. Continue until all vertices have been added.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: primJarnik

label: divide and conquer
summary: NIST DADS defines divide and conquer as: Solve a problem, either directly because solving that instance is easy (typically, because the instance is small) or by dividing it into two or more smaller instances. Each of these smaller instances is recursively solved, and the solutions are combined to produce a solution for the original instance.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: divideAndConquer

label: backtracking
summary: NIST DADS defines backtracking as: Find a solution by trying one of several choices. If the choice proves incorrect, computation backtracks or restarts at the point of choice and tries another choice. It is often convenient to maintain choice points and alternate choices using recursion .

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: backtrack

label: trie
summary: NIST DADS defines trie as: A tree for storing strings in which there is one node for every common prefix . The strings are stored in extra leaf nodes.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: trie

label: B-tree
summary: NIST DADS defines B-tree as: A balanced search tree in which every node has between ⌈ m/2⌉ and m children , where m>1 is a fixed integer. m is the order . The root may have as few as 2 children. This is a good structure if much of the tree is in slow memory (disk), since the height , and hence the number of accesses, can be kept small, say one or two, by picking a large m. Also known as balanced multiway tree.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: btree

label: finite state machine
summary: NIST DADS defines finite state machine as: A model of computation consisting of a set of states , a start state , an input alphabet , and a transition function that maps input symbols and current states to a next state . Computation begins in the start state with an input string. It changes to new states depending on the transition function. There are many variants, for instance, machines having actions (outputs) associated with transitions ( Mealy machine ) or states ( Moore machine ), multiple start states, transitions conditioned on no input symbol (a null) or more than one transition for a given symbol and state ( nondeterministic finite state machine ), one or more states designated as accepting states ( recognizer ), etc. Also known as finite state automaton.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: finiteStateMachine

label: balanced binary tree
summary: NIST DADS defines balanced binary tree as: A binary tree where no leaf is more than a certain amount farther from the root than any other. After inserting or deleting a node , the tree may rebalanced with rotations .

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: balancedbitr

label: priority queue
summary: NIST DADS defines priority queue as: An abstract data type to efficiently support finding the item with the highest priority across a series of operations. The basic operations are: insert, find-minimum (or maximum), and delete-minimum (or maximum). Some implementations also efficiently support join two priority queues ( meld ), delete an arbitrary item, and increase the priority of a item (decrease-key). Formal Definition: The operations new(), insert(v, PQ), find-minimum or min(PQ), and delete-minimum or dm(PQ) may be defined with axiomatic semantics as follows. new() returns a priority queue min(insert(v, new())) = v dm(insert(v, new())) = new() min(insert(v, insert(w, PQ))) = if priority(v) < priority(min(insert(w, PQ))) then v else min(insert(w, PQ)) dm(insert(v, insert(w, PQ))) = if priority(v) < priority(min(insert(w, PQ))) then insert(w, PQ) else insert(v, dm(insert(w, PQ))) where PQ is a priority queue, v and w are items, and priority(v) is the priority of item v.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: priorityque

label: hash table
summary: NIST DADS defines hash table as: A dictionary in which keys are mapped to array positions by hash functions . Having the keys of more than one item map to the same position is called a collision . There are many collision resolution schemes , but they may be divided into open addressing , chaining , and keeping one special overflow area. Perfect hashing avoids collisions, but may be time-consuming to create. Also known as scatter storage.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: hashtab

label: breadth-first search
summary: NIST DADS defines breadth-first search as: Any search algorithm that considers neighbors of a vertex , that is, outgoing edges of the vertex's predecessor in the search, before any outgoing edges of the vertex. Extremes are searched last. This is typically implemented with a queue .

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: breadthfirst

label: depth-first search
summary: NIST DADS defines depth-first search as: (1) Any search algorithm that considers outgoing edges ( children ) of a vertex before any of the vertex's siblings , that is, outgoing edges of the vertex's predecessor in the search. Extremes are searched first. This is easily implemented with recursion . (2) An algorithm that marks all vertices in a directed graph in the order they are discovered and finished, partitioning the graph into a forest . Also known as DFS.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: depthfirst

label: Kruskal's algorithm
summary: NIST DADS defines Kruskal's algorithm as: An algorithm for computing a minimum spanning tree . It maintains a set of partial minimum spanning trees, and repeatedly adds the shortest edge in the graph whose vertices are in different partial minimum spanning trees.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: kruskalsalgo

label: dynamic programming
summary: NIST DADS defines dynamic programming as: Solve an optimization problem by caching subproblem solutions ( memoization ) rather than recomputing them.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: dynamicprog

label: greedy algorithm
summary: NIST DADS defines greedy algorithm as: An algorithm that always takes the best immediate, or local, solution while finding an answer. Greedy algorithms find the overall, or globally, optimal solution for some optimization problems , but may find less-than-optimal solutions for some instances of other problems.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: greedyalgo

label: binary tree
summary: NIST DADS defines binary tree as: A tree with at most two children for each node . Formal Definition: A binary tree either is empty (no nodes), or has a root node, a left binary tree, and a right binary tree. Also known as dyadic tree.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: binarytree

label: directed graph
summary: NIST DADS defines directed graph as: A graph whose edges are ordered pairs of vertices . That is, each edge can be followed from one vertex to another vertex. Formal Definition: A graph G is a pair (V,E), where V is a set of vertices, and E is a set of edges between the vertices E ⊆ {(u,v) | u, v ∈ V}. If the graph does not allow self-loops , adjacency is irreflexive , that is E ⊆ {(u,v) | u, v ∈ V ∧ u ≠ v}. Also known as digraph, oriented graph.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: directedGraph

label: deterministic finite state machine
summary: NIST DADS defines deterministic finite state machine as: A finite state machine with at most one transition for each symbol and state . Also known as DFA, deterministic finite automaton.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: determFinitStateMach

label: nondeterministic finite state machine
summary: NIST DADS defines nondeterministic finite state machine as: A finite state machine whose transition function maps inputs symbols and states to a (possibly empty) set of next states . The transition function also may map the null symbol (no input symbol needed) and states to next states. Also known as NFA, nondeterministic finite automaton.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: nondetermFiniteStateMach

label: array
summary: NIST DADS defines array as: An assemblage of items that are randomly accessible by integers, the index. Formal Definition: Ignoring size an array may be seen as an abstract data type with the operations new(), set(i, v, A), and get(i, A), where i is a numeric index, v is a value, and A is an array. The operations may be defined with axiomatic semantics as follows. new() returns an array get(i, set(i, v, A)) = v get(i, set(j, v, A)) = get(i, A) if i ≠ j Compare this with a dictionary using integers as keys. If the contents of a new array are set to some implicit initial value v i , we could add the following rule for get. get(i, new()) = v i Typically arrays have a fixed size and use either 0-based indexing or 1-based indexing . Fixed initial size and 0-based indexing may incorporated as follows. new(s) returns an array, which has a size s size(new(s)) = s size(set(i, v, A)) = size(A) get(i, set(i, v, A)) = v if 0 ≤ i < size(A) get(i, set(j, v, A)) = get(i, A) if i ≠ j One-based or other indexing may be defined similarly.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: array

label: list
summary: NIST DADS defines list as: A collection of items accessible one after another beginning at the head and ending at the tail .

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: list

label: set
summary: NIST DADS defines set as: An unordered collection of values where each value occurs at most once. A group of elements with three properties: (1) all elements belong to a universe , (2) either each element is a member of the set or it is not, and (3) the elements are unordered. Formal Definition: As an abstract data type , a set has a single query function, isIn(v, S), which tells whether an element is a member of the set or not, and two modifier functions, add(v, S) and remove(v, S). These may be defined with axiomatic semantics as follows. new() returns a set isIn(v, new()) = false isIn(v, add(v, S)) = true isIn(v, add(u, S)) = isIn(v , S) if v ≠ u remove(v, new()) = new() remove(v, add(v, S)) = remove(v, S) remove(v, add(u, S)) = add(u, remove(v, S)) if v ≠ u where S is a set and u and v are elements. The predicate isEmpty(S) may be defined with the following additional axioms. isEmpty(new()) = true isEmpty(add(v, S)) = false

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: set

label: tree
summary: NIST DADS defines tree as: (1) A data structure accessed beginning at the root node. Each node is either a leaf or an internal node . An internal node has one or more child nodes and is called the parent of its child nodes. All children of the same node are siblings . Contrary to a physical tree, the root is usually depicted at the top of the structure, and the leaves are depicted at the bottom. (2) A connected , undirected , acyclic graph . It is rooted and ordered unless otherwise specified. Thanks to Joshua O'Madadhain ( [email protected] ) for the figure, 6 October 2005. Formal Definition: (1) A tree is either empty (no nodes), or a root and zero or more subtrees. The subtrees are ordered.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: tree

label: root
summary: NIST DADS defines root as: The distinguished initial or fundamental item of a tree . The only item which has no parent . See the figure at tree .

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: root

label: leaf
summary: NIST DADS defines leaf as: A node in a tree without any children . See the figure at tree . Also known as external node, terminal node.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: leaf

label: edge
summary: NIST DADS defines edge as: A connection between two vertices of a graph . In a weighted graph , each edge has an number, called a "weight". In a directed graph , an edge goes from one vertex, the source , to another, the target , and hence makes connection in only one direction. Also known as arc.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: edge

label: vertex
summary: NIST DADS defines vertex as: An item in a graph . Sometimes referred to as a node .

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: vertex

label: path
summary: NIST DADS defines path as: A list of vertices of a graph where each vertex has an edge between it and the next vertex.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: path

label: cycle
summary: NIST DADS defines cycle as: A path that starts and ends at the same vertex and includes at least one edge .

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: cycle

label: weighted graph
summary: NIST DADS defines weighted graph as: A graph having a weight, or number, associated with each edge . Some algorithms require all weights to be nonnegative, integral, positive, etc. Also known as edge-weighted graph.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: weightedGraph

label: connected graph
summary: NIST DADS defines connected graph as: An undirected graph that has a path between every pair of vertices .

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: connectedGraph

label: complete graph
summary: NIST DADS defines complete graph as: An undirected graph with an edge between every pair of vertices .

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: completeGraph

label: bipartite graph
summary: NIST DADS defines bipartite graph as: An undirected graph where vertices can be partition ed into two sets such that no edge connects vertices in the same set.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: bipartgraph

label: directed acyclic graph
summary: NIST DADS defines directed acyclic graph as: A directed graph with no path that starts and ends at the same vertex . Also known as DAG, acyclic directed graph, oriented acyclic graph.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: directAcycGraph

label: abstract data type
summary: NIST DADS defines abstract data type as: A set of data values and associated operations that are precisely specified independent of any particular implementation. Also known as ADT.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: abstractDataType

label: circular list
summary: NIST DADS defines circular list as: A variant of a linked list in which the nominal tail is linked to the head . The entire list may be accessed starting at any item and following links until one comes to the starting item again.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: circularlist

label: circular queue
summary: NIST DADS defines circular queue as: An implementation of a bounded queue using an array .

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: circularQueue

label: deque
summary: NIST DADS defines deque as: A data structure in which items may be added to or deleted from the head or the tail . Also known as doubly-ended queue.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: deque

label: binary heap
summary: NIST DADS defines binary heap as: A complete binary tree where every node has a key more extreme (greater or less) than or equal to the key of its parent .

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: binaryheap

label: Fibonacci heap
summary: NIST DADS defines Fibonacci heap as: A heap made of a forest of trees . The amortized cost of the operations create, insert a value, decrease a value, find minimum, and merge or join ( meld ) two heaps, is a constant Θ(1) . The delete operation takes O(log n) .

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: fibonacciHeap

label: binomial heap
summary: NIST DADS defines binomial heap as: A heap made of a forest of binomial trees with the heap property numbered k=0, 1, 2, …, n, each containing either 0 or 2 k nodes . Each tree is formed by linking two of its predecessors, by joining one at the root of the other. The operations of insert a value, decrease a value, delete a value, and merge or join ( meld ) two queues take O(log n) time. The find minimum operation is a constant Θ(1) .

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: binomialheap

label: splay tree
summary: NIST DADS defines splay tree as: A binary search tree in which operations that access nodes restructure the tree.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: splaytree

label: 2-3 tree
summary: NIST DADS defines 2-3 tree as: A B-tree of order 3, that is, internal nodes have two or three children .

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: two3tree

label: suffix tree
summary: NIST DADS defines suffix tree as: A compact representation of a trie corresponding to the suffixes of a given string where all nodes with one child are merged with their parents .

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: suffixtree

label: suffix array
summary: NIST DADS defines suffix array as: An array of all starting positions of suffixes of a string arranged in lexicographical order . This allows a binary search or fast substring search.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: suffixarray

label: hash function
summary: NIST DADS defines hash function as: A function that maps keys to integers, usually to get an even distribution on a smaller set of values. Also known as hash.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: hash

label: perfect hashing
summary: NIST DADS defines perfect hashing as: A hash function that maps each different key to a distinct integer. Usually all possible keys must be known beforehand. A hash table that uses a perfect hash has no collisions . Formal Definition: A function f is perfect for a set of keys K iff ∀ j, k ∈ K f(j) = f(k) → j = k. Also known as optimal hashing.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: perfecthash

label: open addressing
summary: NIST DADS defines open addressing as: A class of collision resolution schemes in which all items are stored within the hash table . In case of collision , other positions are computed, giving a probe sequence , and checked until an empty position is found. Some ways of computing possible new positions are less efficient because of clustering . Typically items never move once put in place, but in Robin Hood hashing , LCFS hashing , and other techniques, previously placed items may move.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: openAddressing

label: linear probing
summary: NIST DADS defines linear probing as: A hash table in which a collision is resolved by putting the item in the next empty place in the array following the occupied place. Even with a moderate load factor , primary clustering tends to slow retrieval.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: linearprobng

label: double hashing
summary: NIST DADS defines double hashing as: A method of open addressing for a hash table in which a collision is resolved by searching the table for an empty place at intervals given by a different hash function, thus minimizing clustering . Also known as rehashing.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: doublehashng

label: cuckoo hashing
summary: NIST DADS defines cuckoo hashing as: A dictionary implemented with two hash tables , T 1 and T 2 , and two different hash functions , h 1 and h 2 . Each key , k, is either in T 1 [h 1 (k)] or T 2 [h 2 (k)]. A new key , k, is stored in T 1 [h 1 (k)]. If that location is already occupied by another key, l, the other key is moved to T 2 [h 2 (l)]. Keys are moved back and forth until a key moves to an empty location or a limit is reached. If the limit is reached, new hash functions are chosen, and the tables are rehashed. For tables that are a bit less than half full and with carefully chosen universal hashing functions, performance is good. A key is deleted by removing it from a table.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: cuckooHashing

label: recursion
summary: NIST DADS defines recursion as: An algorithmic technique where a function, in order to accomplish a task, calls itself with some part of the task.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: recursion

label: iteration
summary: NIST DADS defines iteration as: Solve a problem by repeatedly working on successive parts of the problem.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: iteration

label: memoization
summary: NIST DADS defines memoization as: Save (memoize) a computed answer for possible later reuse, rather than recomputing the answer.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: memoize

label: branch and bound
summary: NIST DADS defines branch and bound as: An algorithmic technique to find the optimal solution by keeping the best solution found so far. If a partial solution cannot improve on the best, it is abandoned.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: branchNbound

label: exhaustive search
summary: NIST DADS defines exhaustive search as: An algorithm that finds a solution by trying every possibility.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: exhaustiveSearch

label: interpolation search
summary: NIST DADS defines interpolation search as: Search a sorted array by estimating the next position to check based on a linear interpolation of the search key and the values at the ends of the search interval. Also known as extrapolation search.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: interpolationSearch

label: jump search
summary: NIST DADS defines jump search as: Search a sorted array by checking every j th item until the right area is found, then doing a linear search . The optimum for n items is when j=√ n. Also known as block search.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: jumpsearch

label: Fibonaccian search
summary: NIST DADS defines Fibonaccian search as: Search a sorted array by narrowing possible locations to progressively smaller intervals. Begin with two Fibonacci numbers , p (F(n)) and q (F(n+1)), such that p < n ≤ q, where n is the size of the array. The first step checks location p. The size of the next interval is p, if the key is less than the item at that location, or q-p (F(n-1)) if it is greater.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: fibonaccianSearch

label: all pairs shortest path
summary: NIST DADS defines all pairs shortest path as: Find the weight (or length) of the shortest paths between all pairs of vertices in a weighted, directed graph .

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: allPairsShortestPath

label: transitive closure
summary: NIST DADS defines transitive closure as: An extension or superset of a binary relation such that whenever (a,b) and (b,c) are in the extension, (a,c) is also in the extension.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: transitiveClosure

label: Euclid's algorithm
summary: NIST DADS defines Euclid's algorithm as: An algorithm to compute the greatest common divisor of two positive integers. It is Euclid(a,b){if (b=0) then return a; else return Euclid(b, a mod b);} . The run time complexity is O((log a)(log b)) bit operations. Also known as Euclidean algorithm.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: euclidalgo

label: fast fourier transform
summary: NIST DADS defines fast fourier transform as: An algorithm to convert a set of uniformly spaced points from the time domain to the frequency domain. Also known as FFT.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: fastFourierTransform

label: Huffman coding
summary: NIST DADS defines Huffman coding as: A minimal variable-length character coding based on the frequency of each character. First, each character becomes a one-node binary tree , with the character as the only node . The character's frequency is the tree's frequency. Two trees with the least frequencies are joined as the subtrees of a new root that is assigned the sum of their frequencies. Repeat until all characters are in one tree. One code bit represents each level . Thus more frequent characters are near the root and are coded with few bits, and rare characters are far from the root and are coded with many bits. Also known as static Huffman coding.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: huffmanCoding

label: arithmetic coding
summary: NIST DADS defines arithmetic coding as: A minimal variable-length message coding based on the frequency of each character. The message is represented by a fraction which is the repeated offset-plus-product reduction of the range (offset) and probability (product) of each character.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: arithmeticCoding

label: Lempel-Ziv-Welch
summary: NIST DADS defines Lempel-Ziv-Welch as: A compression algorithm that codes strings of characters with codes of a fixed number of bits. Every new string in the input is added to a table until it is full. The codes of existing strings are output instead of the strings. Also known as LZW compression.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: lempelZivWelch

label: string matching
summary: NIST DADS defines string matching as: The problem of finding occurrence(s) of a pattern string within another string or body of text. There are many different algorithms for efficient searching. Also known as exact string matching, string searching, text searching.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: stringMatching

label: Boyer-Moore
summary: NIST DADS defines Boyer-Moore as: A string matching algorithm that compares characters from the end of the pattern to its beginning. When characters don't match, searching jumps to the next possible match: the farthest of a table like that used in the Knuth-Morris-Pratt algorithm and the next matching position in the pattern .

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: boyermoore

label: Shell sort
summary: NIST DADS defines Shell sort as: The first diminishing increment sort . On each pass i sets of n/i items are sorted, typically with insertion sort . On each succeeding pass, i is reduced until it is 1 for the last pass. A good series of i values is important to efficiency.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: shellsort

label: comb sort
summary: NIST DADS defines comb sort as: An in-place sort algorithm that repeatedly reorders different pairs of items. On each pass swap pairs of items separated by the increment or gap, if needed, and reduce the gap (divide it by about 1.3). The gap starts at about 3/4 of the number of items. Continue until the gap is 1 and a pass had no swaps.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: combSort

label: gnome sort
summary: NIST DADS defines gnome sort as: Put items in order by comparing the current item with the previous item. If they are in order, move to the next item (or stop if the end is reached). If they are out of order, swap them and move to the previous item. If there is no previous item, move to the next item.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: gnomeSort

label: in-place sort
summary: NIST DADS defines in-place sort as: A sort algorithm in which the sorted items occupy the same storage as the original ones. These algorithms may use o(n) additional memory for bookkeeping, but at most a constant number of items are kept in auxiliary memory at any time. Also known as sort in place.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: inplacesort

label: comparison sort
summary: NIST DADS defines comparison sort as: Any sort algorithm using comparisons between keys , and nothing else about the keys, to arrange items in a predetermined order. An alternative is a restricted universe sort such as counting sort or bucket sort .

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: comparisnsrt

label: external sort
summary: NIST DADS defines external sort as: Any sort algorithm that uses external memory, such as tape or disk, during the sort. Since most common sort algorithms assume high-speed random access to all intermediate memory, they are unsuitable if the values to be sorted don't fit in main memory.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: externalsort

label: internal sort
summary: NIST DADS defines internal sort as: Any sort algorithm which uses exclusively main memory during the sort. This assumes high-speed random access to all memory.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: internalsort

label: bitonic sort
summary: NIST DADS defines bitonic sort as: Compare, and swap if necessary, pairs of elements in parallel. Subsets are sorted then merged. Also known as Batcher sort.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: bitonicSort

label: finite state transducer
summary: NIST DADS defines finite state transducer as: A finite state machine specifically with a read-only input and a write-only output. The input and output cannot be reread or changed.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: finiteStateTransducer

label: Turing machine
summary: NIST DADS defines Turing machine as: A model of computation consisting of a finite state machine controller, a read-write head, and an unbounded sequential tape. Depending on the current state and symbol read on the tape, the machine can change its state and move the head to the left or right. Unless otherwise specified, a Turing machine is deterministic .

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: turingMachine

label: nondeterministic Turing machine
summary: NIST DADS defines nondeterministic Turing machine as: A Turing machine which has more than one next state for some combinations of contents of the current cell and current state. An input is accepted if any move sequence leads to acceptance.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: nondetermTuringMach

label: big-O notation
summary: NIST DADS defines big-O notation as: A theoretical measure of the execution of an algorithm , usually the time or memory needed, given the problem size n, which is usually the number of items. Informally, saying some equation f(n) = O(g(n)) means it is less than some constant multiple of g(n). The notation is read, "f of n is big oh of g of n". Formal Definition: f(n) = O(g(n)) means there are positive constants c and k, such that 0 ≤ f(n) ≤ cg(n) for all n ≥ k. The values of c and k must be fixed for the function f and must not depend on n. Also known as O, asymptotic upper bound.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: bigOnotation

label: asymptotic bound
summary: NIST DADS defines asymptotic bound as: A curve representing the limit of a function. That is, the distance between a function and the curve tends to zero. The function may or may not intersect the bounding curve.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: asymptoticBound

label: NP-complete
summary: NIST DADS defines NP-complete as: The complexity class of decision problems for which answers can be checked for correctness, given a certificate , by an algorithm whose run time is polynomial in the size of the input (that is, it is NP ) and no other NP problem is more than a polynomial factor harder. Informally, a problem is NP-complete if answers can be verified quickly, and a quick algorithm to solve this problem can be used to solve all other NP problems quickly.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: npcomplete

label: polynomial time
summary: NIST DADS defines polynomial time as: When the execution time of a computation, m(n), is no more than a polynomial function of the problem size, n. More formally m(n) = O(n k ) where k is a constant.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: polynomialtm
